content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published a guide in 2018 titled Integrating Palliative Care and Symptom Relief into Primary Health Care: A WHO Guide for Planners, Implementers, and Managers. This document emphasizes the importance of integrating palliative care into primary health care (PHC) systems to address the significant global disparities in access to palliative care services. It highlights that palliative care is an ethical responsibility of health systems and a critical component of universal health coverage (UHC). Palliative care, as defined by WHO, involves the prevention and relief of suffering for patients and their families facing life-threatening illnesses. This care addresses physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering. It aims to improve quality of life, promote dignity, and provide comfort while supporting patients and families throughout the course of illness. Palliative care is not limited to end-of-life care but is applicable early in the course of illness, alongside curative or life-prolonging treatments. It also supports bereaved family members after a patient’s death, if needed. The guide underscores that most people requiring palliative care prefer to remain at home, making it essential to provide such care in the community as part of PHC. It is neither feasible nor necessary for palliative care specialists to provide the majority of care. Instead, primary care providers with basic training in palliative care can effectively address most needs and refer patients to higher levels of care when required. Despite the effectiveness of palliative care in alleviating suffering, access remains limited, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). For example, in 2013, 91% of the world’s morphine consumption occurred in high-income countries (HICs), which represent only 19% of the global population. In contrast, LMICs, home to 81% of the population, consumed only 9%. This disparity highlights the urgent need to improve access to essential medicines like morphine, which is critical for managing moderate to severe pain. Barriers to palliative care include a lack of national policies, strategic plans, and clinical guidelines; insufficient training programs; limited insurance coverage for home-based care; and restrictive opioid prescribing regulations. Additionally, misconceptions about palliative care—such as the belief that it is only for the dying or that it substitutes disease prevention and treatment—further hinder its development and accessibility. The WHO guide provides practical recommendations for integrating palliative care into PHC systems. It outlines an Essential Package of Palliative Care for PHC, which includes basic training for primary care providers, access to essential medicines (e.g., oral and injectable morphine), and community-based services. The integration of palliative care into PHC aligns with the WHO Framework on Integrated, People-Centered Health Services, which prioritizes primary and community care services. By strengthening PHC systems, palliative care can improve health outcomes, reduce suffering, and promote equity in access to essential health services. In conclusion, the WHO guide serves as a valuable resource for health ministries, planners, and managers to incorporate palliative care into PHC systems. It reiterates WHO’s commitment to addressing the needs of vulnerable populations and ensuring that everyone has access to compassionate, high-quality care.
